questions.stem: A robot continuously draws 10 W for motors, 5 W for computing and 5 W for sensors. Its battery is modeled as a fully usable 12 V × 2.5 Ah energy store, with no additional losses. What are the stored energy and ideal runtime?
questions.subtopic: Ideal battery runtime and energy budget
assumptions: Constant stated voltage and powers; full nominal energy usable; ignore conversion losses, reserves and discharge-rate effects.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 50: Week 11 item 1, battery/load prompt and energy/runtime working
citations.evidenceText: Motor 10 W, compute 5 W, sensors 5 W; 12 V, 2.5 Ah; energy 30 Wh and constant-load runtime 1.5 h = 90 min.

solution.justification: Convert battery charge capacity to energy, add simultaneous loads, then divide energy by power. This is an ideal estimate, not a measured battery-life promise.

optionExplanations.o1: Energy is 12×2.5=30 Wh; total load is 20 W, giving 1.5 h or 90 min.
optionExplanations.o2: 180 min neglects the combined 10 W computing and sensor load.
optionExplanations.o3: Ampere-hours are charge capacity, not watt-hours; the voltage factor was omitted.
optionExplanations.o4: 1.5 is the runtime in hours, not minutes.

assumptions: Constant loads and voltage; all stated energy available; no extra losses.

questions.stem: Use an ideal 10-bit ADC with 5 V reference and the explicit quantizer k=floor(1024 Vᵢₙ/5) for 0≤Vᵢₙ<5 V. A display reconstructs voltage as V̂=5k/1023. If k=1023, which pair gives the display value and the possible input interval?
questions.subtopic: ADC top bin versus endpoint estimate
assumptions: The quantizer and reconstruction equations are supplied modeling conventions, not a universal Arduino specification; no saturation or noise; input below 5 V.

options.text: V̂=5 V; Vᵢₙ must equal exactly 5 V.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 51: Week 11 item 3, maximum ADC code and 0–5 V explanation
citations.evidenceText: The original gives code 1023 and keys 5 V; its explanation supplies a 0–5 V, 0–1023 convention without distinguishing code-bin uncertainty.

solution.justification: A digital code identifies a quantization bin, not one exact analog voltage. The explicit model makes the endpoint display convention and the top input interval separately testable.

optionExplanations.o1: The endpoint reconstruction is 5 V, but floor quantization maps a finite top bin to code 1023.
optionExplanations.o2: This confuses the displayed endpoint estimate with a uniquely determined input; exactly 5 V is outside the stated domain.
optionExplanations.o3: This substitutes a 3.3 V reference despite the explicitly fixed 5 V model.
optionExplanations.o4: This treats the maximum code as a midpoint code and therefore selects the wrong interval.

citations.evidenceText: 600 PPR and 1800 pulses produce 3 rotations when counted pulses use the stated PPR convention.

optionExplanations.o2: The fourfold count density must divide the inferred rotations, not multiply them.
optionExplanations.o3: This assigns the four-count mode to A and one-count mode to B.
optionExplanations.o4: This ignores the explicitly different counting conventions.

questions.stem: Assume motor torque decreases continuously with positive shaft speed, opposing load torque is constant, and the curves meet at ω*. With positive inertia and unchanged curves, the motor is momentarily at a speed just below ω*. What follows?
assumptions: Strictly decreasing motor torque locally; constant opposing load; positive inertia; no changed voltage, load or controller mode.

options.text: Motor torque is below load torque, so speed initially decreases away from ω*.
Motor and load torque remain equal, so the lower speed is another equilibrium.
Motor torque exceeds load torque, so speed initially increases toward ω*.
Motor torque exceeds load torque, so speed initially decreases toward zero.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 52: Week 11 item 6, below-equilibrium prompt and highlighted torque comparison
citations.evidenceText: Below the source’s operating point, motor torque exceeds load torque and the system accelerates toward it.

solution.justification: Speed is pulled toward this stable crossing because the motor has a torque surplus below it. The curve assumptions matter; “below equilibrium” alone does not determine stability for every possible load curve.

optionExplanations.o1: A decreasing motor curve has higher torque below its intersection with the constant load, leaving positive accelerating torque.
optionExplanations.o2: This reverses the inequality implied by the decreasing motor curve.
optionExplanations.o3: The stipulated decrease and constant load give an isolated crossing, not equality at every nearby speed.
optionExplanations.o4: This gets the torque ordering right but reverses the sign of angular acceleration.

assumptions: Positive J; stated local torque curves; both torques referred to the same shaft.

questions.stem: A one-dimensional classifier uses f(x)=2.5x−7.5, with x measured in mm/s; positive f means Normal (+1), negative f means Faulty (−1). Define signed geometric distance as displacement along increasing x from the boundary f(x)=0. At x=3.2 mm/s, which tuple (class, decision score, signed geometric distance) is correct?
questions.subtopic: SVM decision score versus geometric distance
assumptions: One unscaled feature axis; score is dimensionless, so slope 2.5 has units (mm/s)⁻¹; positive distance is toward increasing x; x is not on the boundary.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 53: Week 11 item 8, classifier, measurement, answer pairs and calculation
citations.evidenceText: f(x)=2.5x−7.5, x=3.2 mm/s; Normal is +1. Highlighted option A says Normal, distance=0.5; working computes f(3.2)=0.5.

solution.justification: The class depends on the sign of the score. Geometric distance depends on the location of the boundary in feature units. The source’s 0.5 calculation is a decision score, not the requested feature-space distance.

optionExplanations.o1: The boundary is x=3; f(3.2)=0.5>0, and the displacement is 3.2−3=+0.2 mm/s.
optionExplanations.o2: This mistakes the unnormalized decision score for a geometric distance.
optionExplanations.o3: Both the score sign and the position relative to the boundary are reversed.
optionExplanations.o4: This swaps the numerical roles of score and geometric distance.

steps: Signed displacement d=x−x₀=0.2 mm/s; equivalently f/|2.5|=0.2 mm/s.

variables.d: signed geometric distance toward increasing x

assumptions: One-dimensional unscaled feature; a>0; Euclidean feature-space displacement.

misconceptions: This mistakes the unnormalized decision score for a geometric distance.
Both the score sign and the position relative to the boundary are reversed.

assumptions: Centering and scaling enabled; finite nonconstant training feature; population variance; same fitted transformation reused without refitting.

options.text: Every new input batch has mean zero and variance one, even though no statistics are refitted.
The transformed training feature has mean zero and variance one; a new input batch need not have either statistic.
It maps every training value into [0,1] and preserves that interval for every new input.
It constrains the predicted output torque to be nonnegative while leaving input scale unchanged.

citations.evidenceText: The prompt asks why input StandardScaler precedes inverse-dynamics MLPRegressor.

citations.locator: Assignment physical page 54: Week 11 item 9 continuation, options and printed answer
citations.evidenceText: The source identifies zero-mean, unit-variance input normalization.

solution.justification: Use the training data to establish a common feature scale. The nonconstant-feature and fitted-training-data qualifications prevent an overbroad “all data always has unit variance” claim.
